paper_title: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: AI agents deployed on the open web are becoming more capable of performing actions that may breach contractual provisions and violate computer security laws. In this paper, we introduce ScrapeBench, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the legal compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies, namely terms of service (ToS) and $\texttt{robots.txt}$ directives. Across widely used closed-weight and open-weight AI agents, we find that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. In addition, we observe that even where AI agents actively check the applicable ToS and $\texttt{robots.txt}$, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates. Conversely, in our sample of 269 websites that do not prohibit scraping, we observe that agents sometimes refuse to scrape despite it being lawful, such as Claude Opus 4.6 exhibiting an over-refusal rate of 98.5%. Our human baseline experiments (n = 180 participants) suggest that humans exhibit compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: AI agents built atop large language models (LLMs) can increasingly reason, use tools, and take variety of actions in online environments [4, 5]. As these agents begin to act more autonomously, their actions implicate growing range of legal frameworks and rules, including those that govern access and use of online content [20, 21, 29, 7, 19, 6, 23]. One such common activity is scraping, i.e., the automated collection of website content [12, 16, 34]. Popular websites such as Amazon, ESPN, and The New York Times often prohibit scraping through legally binding contracts, in the form of terms of service (ToS) and robots.txt directives [17, 5, 3, 1, 31, 13, 26] . Whether AI agents comply with these legal restrictions is an open empirical question. At present, most agentic benchmarks focus on performance-oriented metrics, including measuring web-related skills such as information search and retrieval [39, 9, 27], web visual comprehension [24, 38, 18], and work task navigation [8, 40, 11]. These benchmarks often disregard the lawfulness or legal alignment [21, 35] of an AI agents actions, focusing only on whether it accomplishes the tasks [28, 37, 14, 25, 22, 15, 32]. Concretely, an AI agent may successfully scrape websites at scale, but do so in manner that violates applicable law [20, 28, 10, 22]. The problem is compounded by users who may deliberately instruct agents to dismiss legal rules (e.g., Please scrape this website and ignore the terms.). To fill this gap, we introduce SCRAPEBENCH, the first agentic benchmark to empirically evaluate the compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies. Unlike performance-oriented web agent benchmarks that score AI agents based on task completion, SCRAPEBENCH measures whether agents comply with legal constraints, focusing specifically on prohibitions on scraping specified in websites ToS and robots.txt. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. Benchmark Dataset: We curate novel real-world dataset of the ToS and robots.txt directives for the 1,895 most-visited websites, analyzing and annotating which websites prohibit scraping (n = 1,626 websites) and which do not prohibit scraping (n = 269 websites). 2. Agentic Evaluation Framework: We develop an evaluation framework to measure the legal compliance and over-refusal of AI agents under different conditions, including variety of user instructions and varying levels of access to relevant legal resources. We evaluate and report the results for six openand closed-weight AI agents: GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5, Qwen3 Max, and Grok 4.2. 3. Empirical Findings: We find that under neutral prompts, AI agents frequently violate scraping prohibitions, exhibiting compliance rate of < 5%. With few notable exceptions, we generally find relatively low rates of over-refusal in the case of websites that do not prohibit scraping. 4. Human Baseline: To contextualize our findings regarding AI agents, we conduct human baseline for legal compliance in website scraping (n = 180 participants) across three different legal contexts.

sections.title: 2 Building SCRAPEBENCH
sections.content: 2.1 Website Data Pipeline Website Collection and Filtering For our initial unfiltered collection of websites, we extract1 the top 3,000 global websites from the Chrome Top Million Websites (CrUX)2 repository for February 2026. This repository caches the most visited websites, with millions of monthly visits, from the Google BigQuery database and is considered more accurate than commercial third-party top website lists [33]. To standardize the properties and filter the list of websites, we set up the following filtering criteria for removal: (1) NSFW websites such as adult-related content; (2) websites primarily written in non-English languages; and (3) websites with country-specific access restrictions unreachable from the United States. After filtering, total of 1,895 websites were collected for the final dataset. 1To preserve the real-world distribution of top websites, we include all nEP = 1,626 and nNEP = 269 websites in our sample, instead of filtering those to create an artificially (yet unrealistically) balanced dataset. 2https://developer.chrome.com/docs/crux/ Figure 2: Breakdown of website data for SCRAPEBENCH (ntotal = 1,895, nEP = 1,626, nNEP = 269) over domain categories and scraping permissibility. Website Scraping Policies To collect each websites legal policies on scraping based on its ToS3 and robots.txt files, we developed an automated Python scraper using the Beautiful Soup 4.4.0 package. This script iterates over each domain and retrieves its corresponding robots.txt file (often at https://domain.com/robots.txt) and searches over potential subdomain locations of its terms, including /terms, /legal, /tos. Around 30% of the websites have third-party DDoS protection, such as Cloudflare, which blocks automated scrapers from accessing any form of the websites content, including the terms of service. For these websites, we manually visited them via web browser and retrieved the ToS. We note that of the 1,895 websites in our sample, 139 have no ToS and 77 have no robots.txt. 2.2 Data Extraction and Labeling To determine whether website prohibits automated scraping of its content, we prompt GPT-5.2 to extract verbatim text snippets from the entire content of its ToS and robots.txt files that mention forms of automated scraping. We4 identify two scraping permissibility labels5, namely: EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (EP) and NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (NEP), as reported in Table 1 and cross-tabulated in Table 2. For website to be labeled as EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED, either the ToS or the robots.txt must explicitly prohibit any form of scraping as stated in Table 1; otherwise, they will be labeled NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED. For simplicity in our experiments, we removed the websites from our data that do not satisfy the strict binary labeling such as having conditional restrictions on scraping under their ToS or robots.txt. We provide the exact prompts for the labeling process with GPT-5.2 in Appendix B.3. 2.3 Quality Checks Based on the criteria and preprocessing steps discussed above, our final website dataset distribution is reported in Table 2, with 269 websites classified as NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED and 1,626 websites as EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED. To perform final quality check, we randomly sampled 15% of the website data from each category and manually labeled their ToS and robots.txt based on the same criteria in Table 2. We then compared GPT-5.2s labeling of scraping permissibility with ours and found it to be consistently accurate at 97.9% and 98.9% agreement (Cohens κ = 0.91) for ToS and robots.txt, respectively. 3The documents that govern the legal use of websites content include terms of service and terms of use, as well as website privacy policies. For consistency, we use the term terms of service to describe these. 4Two of the co-authors are legal professionals. sections.title: 4 Overall Agentic Compliance and Over-Refusal in Website Scraping
sections.content: 4.1 Measuring Compliance with EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (EP) Websites We evaluate AI agents rate of compliance with websites scraping policies on the EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED websites (n = 1,626). We report compliance rates across all eight prompt conditions and AI agents in Figure 3. Result 1: Using the simplest prompt, AI agents often violate website scraping policies. Under neutral baseline prompt (P1), compliance is near zero for five of six AI agents, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, and Qwen, except for Grok, which achieves 11% compliance. Implicitly mentioning that some websites have scraping policies (P2) does not improve compliance, with the highest being Grok and Kimi, achieving 5.5%-5.7% compliance. Using explicit instructions (P3) and linking the ToS and robots.txt (P4) increase Claudes compliance to 40.1% and 41.5%. Substantially higher compliance is exhibited only when the ToS and robots.txt are pasted as in-context information in the prompt (P5), where GPT, Claude, and Gemini all surpass 70% compliance, while Qwen remains consistently unresponsive with compliance remaining at 2.9%. Result 2: AI agents require strong legal warnings to be compliant. To induce the strongest pressure for compliance, the legal warning prompt (P7) combines the ToS and robots.txt texts, strict instructions to comply, and reference to the applicable law that may be violated. This prompt yields the highest observed compliance rates in five out of six agents, specifically Claude (85.9%), Gemini (85.7%), Kimi (62.7%), Grok (59.7%) and Qwen (13.8%). GPT peaks at P5 (73.9%) while dropping at P7 (60.6%). While these results may suggest that compliance can be partially addressed through prompt engineering, doing so is labor-intensive, as it may require an end-user to paste the full legal texts from the ToS and robots.txt and provide additional instructions. Result 3: Adversarial prompting reduces compliance for most AI agents, with one exception. Under the adversarial prompt (P8) that instructs agents to ignore the ToS and robots.txt, most AI agents exhibit very low compliance, with Gemini down to 41.6%, GPT to 11.7%, Kimi to 9.5%, Qwen to 1.7%, and Grok to 0.6%. Only Claude resists the pressure, achieving compliance rate of 99.7%. However, upon manual inspection of Claudes responses under P8, we find that its high resistance to the adversarial prompt is arguably indiscriminate. That is, the model responds with blanket refusal rather than actually reasoning about whether or not the website in fact prohibits scraping, which could possibly be explained by Claudes safety mechanisms being triggered by the prompt Ignore the terms of service. Figure 4: Over-refusal rates of AI agents on NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED websites (n = 269) across eight legal priming prompts. 4.2 Measuring Over-refusal with NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (NEP) Websites We conduct the same experimental setup as above on the NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (n = 269) websites whose ToS do not contain any restrictions on scraping. We report over-refusal rates across all prompt conditions in Figure 4. Result 4: In-context legal resources reduce non-compliance and over-refusal. Relative to P3, the provision of in-context legal resources (P5 and P6) both increases the compliance rates (above) and decreases the over-refusal rates (here) for some agents. Claudes compliance increases from 40.1% to 83.6% and 82.4%, while its over-refusal rates decrease from 16.4% to 8.2% and 6.7%, across conditions P3, P5, and P6, respectively. Gemini follows similar pattern, with compliance increasing from 26.8% to 75.2% and over-refusal decreasing from 12.6% to 1.5%, for conditions P3 and P5. By contrast, over-refusal rates remain below 6% for GPT, Qwen, and Grok. Result 5: Under adversarial prompts, AI agents either refuse broadly or scrape broadly. Agents evaluated under the adversarial prompt (P8) appear to fall into one of two categories. In the first category, agents broadly refuse to scrape. In the second category, agents broadly proceed to scrape. The former includes Claude, which refused 99.7%-98.5% of scraping requests regardless of scraping permissibility, followed by Gemini at smaller magnitude of 41% and 27.7%. The latter group includes GPT, Kimi, Qwen, and Grok, which exhibited compliance below 12% and over-refusal of 5%.

sections.title: 5 Tool Usage and Legal Resources
sections.content: We examine the relationship between the compliance rates of AI agents and the behaviors that should, at least in theory, lead to higher compliance, such as checking websites ToS and robots.txt. We report in Figures 5 and 6 how frequently the AI agents fetched robots.txt and ToS pages, respectively, for each legal priming prompt. Result 6: AI agents stop checking links when legal resources are already in the prompt. Under the strong legal warning (P7), most AI agents stop fetching the ToS and robots.txt even when the links are included. For robots.txt checking, Claude drops from 100% to 1.6%, Gemini from 99.9% to 1.4%, Kimi from 78.7% to 0.3%. For ToS, the pattern is similar, with checking rates decreasing to below 3% for the other four agents, including Claude at 1.3%, Gemini at 0.9%, Kimi at 0.1%, and Grok at 2.9%. By contrast, the checking rate of GPT for ToS and robots.txt remains high, at 58% and 71%, respectively. 7 Figure 5: ToS and robots.txt checking rates for AI agents and humans across select legal priming prompts (P1, P4, P7) for the EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (EP) websites. Figure 6: ToS and robots.txt checking rates for AI agents and humans across select legal priming prompts (P1, P4, P7) for the NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (NEP) websites. Result 7: AI agents fetching of legal resources does not result in higher compliance. We find noteworthy difference between the rate at which agents check legal resources and agents rate of compliance. All six agents retrieve robots.txt at 60% or higher, with GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok achieving near-perfect retrieval at 99%-100% and ToS retrieval at 80% or higher. However, the compliance rate at P4 remains low across all six agents with GPT at 14.2%, Claude at 41.5%, Gemini at 16.6%, Kimi at 4.7%, Qwen at 7.6%, and Grok at 7.9%. striking case we observed is with GPT, which retrieves both the ToS and robots.txt at very high rates of 82.8% and 100%, respectively, while its compliance rate remains at only 14.2%. The percentages are the proportion of trials classified as VIOLATION in which an AI agent explicitly stated its rationale. Result 8: AI agents violate scraping primarily due to misinterpreting the ToS. To better understand the potential causes of noncompliance, we categorize the stated rationales provided by each agent in its outputs in the VIOLATION trials (30 per agent across P1-P7 prompts, = 1, 260) using GPT-5.4-Mini as judge model, as reported in Table 4. Agents provided rationales in 535 trials, i.e., 42.5% of 1,260. We find that the most common rationale, which arises in almost 70% of the violations, relates to agents first reading robots.txt, concluding that there are no restrictions on scraping since they are classified as NEP, and then completely disregarding the ToS. The next most common rationale for noncompliance, which accounts for 18.5% of violations, relates to misreading the ToS classified as EP and interpreting it to permit scraping. Together, these two rationales arise in approximately 88% of violations, which suggests that noncompliance may arguably be attributed more to failures of legal interpretation rather than wholesale rejection or ignorance of websites ToS and robots.txt. sections.title: 6 Human Baseline Results
sections.content: To contextualize the rates of legal compliance that we observe for AI agents, we conduct human baseline in which human participants perform tasks comparable to those assigned to AI agents. Concretely, we recruit 30 participants via Prolific in between-participant setup, totaling 180 participants across both EP and NEP websites, with 30 participants in each of the P1, P4, and P7 prompt conditions. Each participant is given link to an external web app that asks them to decide whether to press button to scrape 15 randomly sampled websites one at time. We provide full details, statistical analyses, and screenshots of the studys web UI in Appendix E. Result 9: Humans are cautious and less responsive to legal priming than AI agents. Under the neutral baseline (P1), human participants exhibit high compliance of 48.9% on EP websites and high over-refusal of 38.9% on NEP websites, as shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4, respectively. Legal priming under conditions P4 and P7 substantially increases compliance on EP websites to 57.3% (p < 0.04) and 65.1% (p < 0.001), respectively. This change, however, is modest relative to that of some AI agents; for example, Claudes compliance rate increased by 85% from P1 to P7. Meanwhile, for over-refusal rates among human participants, the increase from 38.9% under P1 to 42.8% under P4 and 45.8% under P7, as shown in Figure 4, was not statistically significant. Result 10: Humans check legal resources less often than AI agents, but act on what they read. We observe sharp differences in the rates of checking legal resources between human participants and AI agents. When resources are linked (P4) as seen in Figure 5, humans check the ToS 38.9% and 35.3% of the time for EP and NEP websites, respectively. These rates are substantially lower when compared to those of AI agents, which are between 52% and 83% and 27% and 61% for EP and NEP websites, respectively. When prompted with strong legal warning (P7), humans participants rate of checking ToS increases to 57.8% on EP websites (p < 0.001) and 65.8% on NEP websites (p < 0.001) and, for robots.txt, to 38.9% and 58.7%, respectively. When human participants do read the ToS, there is corresponding increase in compliance for EP websites to 67.1%, compared with 55.7% where human participants did not read the ToS (p < 0.001).

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Failure modes in the legal compliance of AI agents. Our findings with respect to compliance, over-refusal, and tool usage in the context of website scraping shed light on several failure modes of AI agents with respect to legal alignment. First, AI agents accessing legal resources such as ToS when available does not necessarily translate into higher levels of compliance. Second, the heavy reliance of AI agents on the ToS being pasted into the prompt while failing to verify it from the live websites could enable prompt injection attacks (e.g., pasting in false or inaccurate ToS) that undermine legal compliance. Third, AI agents remain highly vulnerable to adversarial prompts, as demonstrated in condition P8. Taken together, these findings highlight the need for more concerted efforts and more robust methods of training AI agents to comply with legal rules [21, 20]. The burden of compliance between end-users and model providers. Given that the compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies is substantially shaped by the inclusion or exclusion of the ToS and robots.txt in the prompt, end-users of agents can significantly affect the level of compliance in practice. As end-users often interact with AI agents using simpler instructions closer to P1 and might lack the legal or technical knowledge to construct prompts like those in P5P7, the rate of legal compliance of agents in practice may be far lower than under more careful prompting conditions. Accordingly, it might be appropriate for model providers to be required to themselves take measures to improve legal compliance, such as using system prompts comparable to the prompts in conditions P5P7.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we introduced SCRAPEBENCH, the first agentic benchmark for empirically evaluating the compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies. Our findings expose three failure modes: (1) under neutral prompts, most AI agents in our experiment scrape prohibited websites and only 9 refuse to do so once the ToS and robots.txt are explicitly inserted into prompts; (2) despite frequently checking legal rules, this does not consistently result in AI agents exhibiting higher levels of compliance with those rules; and (3) some agents exhibit high levels of over-refusal, refusing to complete the scraping task despite it being lawful to do so.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Abstract, Introduction Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Limitations Section Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] 13 Justification: This is benchmark and evaluation paper which does not produce nor make use of any theoretical assumptions and mathematical proofs. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sections 2, 3 , and Appendix Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 14 Answer: [Yes] Justification: The links to the project website and the Github repository containing the code and data to run SCRAPEBENCH is found in the first page of this paper. We also provide supplementary information in Section 3.4 and Appendix C. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc /public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 3, Appendix Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Error bars are reported with agentic and human baseline results in Figures 5 and 6. Statistical analyses are reported across results in Section 6 and further expanded in Appendix E. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) 15 The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A.1 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A.3 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We do not release standalone, reusable copies of the website landing pages retrieved by the AI agents during the evaluation process. Website content may appear in the AI agents tool traces but we enforce limit of 8000 characters per fetch to ensure that no full copies were retrieved as whole. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The bundled ToS and robots.txt files are not original work of ours, and the copyright for these texts remains with their respective website owners. We include them as unaltered verbatim reproductions for the sole purpose of research benchmarking of compliance of AI agents under fair use policies and research exception across jurisdictions. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. 17 If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We release SCRAPEBENCH data under two-tier licensing setup. The data from SCRAPEBENCH include the per-domain permissibility labels, cross-tabulation of ToS and robots.txt verdicts, website annotations, prompt taxonomy, and overall experiment results are released under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CCBY-SA-4.0). Meanwhile, the scripts used for model inference, judging, and evaluation from SCRAPEBENCH are licensed under MIT license. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A.1 Guidelines: 18 The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix A.4 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

sections.title: A General Appendix
sections.content: A.1 Ethics Statement Human Baseline Study. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of the Hebrew University. For our human baseline experiments, all participants provided their informed consent (see Figure 7) and received debriefing form upon completion of the task to fully disclose the studys intent with collecting their scraping decisions (see Figure 18). We ensured that our US-based human participants were paid fairly for their work via Prolific. Participants were compensated at flat rate of 9.00 USD and completed the task in 20-40 minutes. Pro-rated, this is equivalent to 12.00 USD per hour and above the US federal minimum wage of 7.25 USD per hour. We do not collect any personally identifiable information (PII) from participants; by default, we record their Prolific IDs upon completion of the assigned tasks for tracking purposes. We provide full details of the human study, including recruitment, statistical analyses, and screenshots of the studys web UI in Appendix E. Web Scraping Task Setup. The human participants recruited from Prolific never performed actual website scraping. The scrape action for humans is performed by clicking scrape button, which displays the HTML text of the website that was manually pre-saved in database rather than triggering an actual script that performs scrape. Thus, no website received automated traffic as consequence of the human study. For the agentic experiments where real HTTP requests are sent to the 1,895 websites we evaluated as part of SCRAPEBENCH, we took the following precautionary measures to ensure the volume of traffic is well within the bounds of legitimate research on web scraping: 1. We set an identifiable User-Agent (AcademicResearchBot/1.0) for all of our agent setup so that any website operators can attribute and block the traffic if desired. 2. We ensured that each consecutive trial with AI agents are sufficiently separated with an interrequest delay of 2.0 seconds to protect website domains from bursty request traffic. 3. We ensured each trial only retrieves minimal number of URLs from domain mostly comprised of the landing page, robots.txt and ToS using cap of = 5 tool invocations which results in small per-domain footprint. 4. We retained only the public-facing legal sources of robots.txt and ToS for distribution and will not publish scraped landing page content of the websites. Indirect Third-Party Access. We note that some models have indirectly accessed websites through third-party reader and proxy services (e.g., r.jina.ai). Specifically, GPT-5.2 retrieved website content in this manner for 21.6% (409) of the website data, where 2.6% of the websites initially blocked the agent. Accessing third-party readers does not change any compliance or over-refusal judgment and is treated the same as direct access. A.2 Limitations Legal Framing. SCRAPEBENCH evaluates compliance of AI agents with website scraping policies. We note that the enforceability of ToS and robots.txt varies across jurisdictions and may depend on factors that we do not evaluate with SCRAPEBENCH. This includes the purpose of scrape; doctrinal concepts in contract, tort, and property law; copyright and preemption; privacy and data protection law; and determining the relevance and applicability of diverse directives, regulations, and statutes (e.g., the U.S. Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and analogous state laws, the EU Digital Services Act, and the EU General Data Protection Regulation) [36]. Accordingly, we do not claim that any specific AI agent models action, prompt, or outcome from this study necessarily constitutes, or does not constitute, legal violation. Single-Agent, Single-Trial, and Single-Turn Setup. SCRAPEBENCH evaluates each trial in isolation, where single AI agent attempts to scrape the landing page of website. We currently do not cover multi-turn, multi-trial, or multi-agent task decomposition due to time and compute costs (see the overall cost of single-trial setup in Appendix C). However, this direct scoping using singleagent, single-turn setup is crucial for the task and benchmark, as it isolates the compliance signal from potential confounds that arise in long-horizon tasks. We do not claim that our findings generalize 20 to open-ended, multi-agent, multi-turn workflows involving AI agents. We leave explorations in this area for future work. Website Data Snapshot. SCRAPEBENCH is composed of 1,895 websites collected from snapshot of the February 2026 top website list from the Chrome Top Million Websites (CrUX) repository. As with any legal contract, we acknowledge that the content of any websites ToS and associated robots.txt may evolve over time through periodic updates. Thus, we encourage users who will be benchmarking future AI agents with SCRAPEBENCH data to re-validate the contents of the ToS and robots.txt by performing another retrieval collection with the code that contains the endto-end extraction of ToS and robots.txt. Moreover, the current website list finalized as part of SCRAPEBENCH is filtered to only represent high-traffic, English, US-accessible websites to ensure that they can be reached by most commercial AI agents. We leave the agentic compliance evaluation of less-recognized, non-English websites for future work. A. Impact Statement SCRAPEBENCH provides reproducible and diagnostic benchmark which can be used by commercial model providers, academic groups, open-source communities, and legal and governance researchers to evaluate how AI agents comply with website scraping policies. By open-sourcing the benchmark data, code, prompts, and AI agent outputs under an appropriate data license of CC BY-SA 4.0, SCRAPEBENCH lowers the barrier for compliance evaluation of open and commercial AI agents. We note the possibility of misuse risk where the per-domain scraping permissibility labels from the ToS and robots.txt from websites that prohibit scraping may be used to train against compliance (e.g., learning which websites explicitly prohibit scraping to evade detection). We explicitly discourage such use of the SCRAPEBENCH dataset. A.4 Declaration of LLM Use In producing this work, we used Grammarly for minor grammar and spelling corrections, Claude Code (Claude 4.6 and 4.7) and ChatGPT (GPT-5.2) for prototyping scripts to run experiments, assistance with formatting LaTeX tables and figures, troubleshooting code, and problems in Matplotlib visualizations. All recommendations and outputs from these LLM-based tools were scrutinized and verified by the authors before integrating into the paper or the studys codebase.

Given URL, returns JSON object containing the HTTP status code, content type, page content, final URL after redirects, and any error message. Text responses are truncated to 8K characters (or approx. 2K tokens) with marker indicating the original length; binary content is replaced with size descriptor. Redirects are followed automatically, and errors (e.g., timeouts or network connection failures) return structured messages in the JSON response rather than raising exceptions, allowing the agent to observe and respond to failures. The request timeout is 15 seconds and the User-Agent is set to AcademicResearchBot/1.0. The tool description provided to the model is deliberately neutral: Fetch the contents of URL via HTTP GET. Returns the HTTP status code, content type, and page content. This tool can be used to fetch any URL or website content pages. This tool description avoids biasing the agent toward or against checking legal resource documents while making the option available. B.3 Scraping Permissibility Identification Classifying permissibility of terms of service (ToS). We use human-verified LLM-based extraction approach with GPT-5.2 (openai/gpt-5.2, accessed via OpenRouter) by processing each ToS file from each website. We prompted GPT-5.2 to scan for scraping-relevant keywords, classify the ToS text into one of three labels (PROHIBITED, PARTIAL, or PERMISSIBLE), and return the extracted verbatim text excerpt that supports the label. The exact system prompt and user prompt used in querying GPT-5.2 are presented in the two colored boxes below. Additionally, we set temperature = 0.0 for GPT-5.2 with the response constrained to JSON only. We manually verified the correctness of the extracted text excerpts from random 15% sample and found no issues with GPT-5.2s extraction performance. In accordance with our scraping permissibility decision scheme as reported in Table 1 in Section 2.2, we removed websites classified as Partial or conditionally prohibited under explicit non-commercial / educational / attribution / reciprocal terms in order to preserve the clear-cut binary property of the final dataset in terms of scraping permissibility. Classifying permissibility of robots.txt. We develop small Python-based rule engine to deterministically identify the permissibility of robots.txt directives from websites. Each robots.txt file is parsed into list of User-agent/Disallow/Allow blocks and wildcard block in the form of User-agent: * and is then inspected. We label website to be EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (EP) if this wildcard block contains Disallow: / without corresponding Allow: / override, as this means the website denies all automated crawlers, bots, or agents access to all subdomains. Likewise, we also consider it EP if site explicitly names an agent to be blocked (e.g., ClaudeBot). In every other case where there are no robots.txt from the website Disallow: or the robots.txt file only has path-level disallows, the domain is labeled NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED (NEP). The data from SCRAPEBENCH, including the per-domain permissibility labels, cross-tabulation of ToS and robots.txt verdicts, website annotations, prompt taxonomy, and overall experiment results, are under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC-BY-SA-4.0). The bundled ToS and robots.txt files are not original work of ours, and the copyright for these texts remains with their respective website owners. We include them as unaltered verbatim reproductions for the sole purpose of research benchmarking of compliance of AI agents under fair use policies and research exceptions across jurisdictions. Meanwhile, the scripts used for model inference, judging, and evaluation from SCRAPEBENCH are licensed under MIT. Hosting and distribution. The full SCRAPEBENCH dataset is currently released in GitHub repository: https://github.com/imperialite/scrapebench. sections.title: E Human Study Appendix
sections.content: E.1 Recruitment We recruited human participants for the baseline study via Prolific. We selected three of the eight legal priming prompts, specifically P1 (neutral), P4 (resource-linked), and P7 (strong legal warning), as conditions that we cross with the two website categories of EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED and NOT EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED. Each condition is assigned sample of = 30 participants, none of whom were eligible to participate in more than one condition to avoid biased results. The full study yields 180 unique participants. Eligibility criteria. We set the following Prolific pre-screening filters to ensure that the participants we accept for the whole study are able to complete the task without any issues in accessing or interacting with the web application and comprehending the goals of the task: Country of residence. United States selected to ensure that the participants are able to access the websites during each trial and aligns with the geographical point of access when the data is collected which is US, as mentioned in Section 2.1. Primary language. English required in order for the participants to be able to fully read and comprehend the website ToS and robots.txt content shown in the web app UI (Figures 1516). Device setup. Desktop or laptop only (mobile and tablet excluded) the web app we developed requires reading multi-paragraph legal text on website preview, which may be impractical or challenging for participants with smaller screens. Participation restriction. No prior submission to any other ScrapeBench condition enforced via Prolifics exclusion-list setting so that each participant is only allowed to participate with one trial from one condition (e.g., P1 on EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED websites), observing the requirement of between-subjects study. Platform cost and participant compensation. For human participant compensation, we ensured that our US-based human participants were paid fairly for their work via Prolific. Participants were compensated at flat rate of $9.00 and completed the task in 20-40 minutes. Pro-rated, this is equivalent to $12.00 per hour and above the US federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. For the overall costs of the human study, including platform costs, we present the breakdown in Table 13. The per-condition cost for each prompt (P1, P4, P7) for = 30 participants is $270 in rewards plus $90 in platform fees, totaling $360. Across all six conditions and two website categories, the study cost $2,160 in total, where $1,620 in participant compensation and $540 in platform fees. Participants are required to tick an explicit consent box before proceeding, and may withdraw their consent at any time without penalty or loss of compensation. At the end of the study, before completion, we present the participants with debriefing form (Figure 18) disclosing the full intent of the study, including the explicit clarification that clicking the scrape button during the task does not trigger any live scripts to scrape the target website. The action behind the scrape button actually just displays manually pre-saved HTML snapshot of the landing page that we had saved in database in advance. This setup ensured that no website received any automated traffic as result of the human study. We have redacted any identifying institutional and PI details from the forms. 30 E.3 Statistical Analyses Power Analysis. Before launching the full study in Prolific, we conducted power analysis of pilot study using P1 on EXPLICITLY PROHIBITED websites with = 10 participants. Our pilot study resulted in baseline compliance of 52.0% with an intra-class correlation (ICC) of 0.558 across each participants 15 binary decisions. To determine the minimum detectable effect across prompt conditions, we conduct 3-condition omnibus χ2 test with 5,000 Monte Carlo iterations with hypothesized step increase of 52% / 62% / 72% for P1, P4, and P7, respectively. We present the results in Table 14, where obtaining statistical power of 80% requires at least = 15 participants. Doubling this to = 30 per condition with simulated power of 95.2% obtains minimum detectable effect of 7pp per step condition, equivalent to 14pp spread between P1 to P7 as reported in Table 15. We therefore decided to recruit = 30 participants per condition for both the full study to achieve statistical power of 95.2% sufficiently above the acceptable conventional value of 80% and be able to reliably detect small effects between each prompt condition by at least 7pp. Table 14: Predicted statistical power of sample sizes from performing 3-condition omnibus χ2 test, assuming 52% / 62% / 72% spread across P1, P4, and P7. per group Total Power 10 15 20 25 30 30 45 60 75 90 120 75.5% 82.5% 88.5% 92.5% 95.2% 97.8% Table 15: Predicted minimum detectable effects (MDE) at = 30 per group, sweeping the per-tier step size while holding P1 = 52% compliance constant. In accordance with the conditions of each legal priming prompt selected for the human baseline task, the amount of legal resources on screen differs for P1, P4, and P7. P1 (Neutral, Figures 89) only shows the domain and the decision panel, P4 (Resource Linked, Figures 1011) additionally shows two clickable buttons that the participants can use to view the websites ToS (Figure 15) and robots.txt (Figure 16) in collapsible side panels, and P7 (Strong Legal Warning, Figures 1213) keeps the same two buttons for viewing ToS and robots.txt and adds legal-warning panel that reproduces the wording of the agentic-experiment P7 prompt (CFAAstyle legal language about potential breach of contract and statutory liability for non-compliance). When participant clicks the Scrape button, the web app displays manually pre-saved HTML text of the landing page of the website (Figure 14). The Scrape button only simulates the scrape function from the participants perspective, but no actual scraping via script to fetch any content and produce website traffic is done during the study. Upon completion of scraping decisions from the 15 websites, an optional open-ended feedback request is shown to participants (Figure 17) before presenting the debriefing form (Figure 18), which closes the task and session.
